title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 14
paragraphs: In this way the Mermnadae gained the throne, ousting the Heraclids. When Gyges became ruler, he sent a good many votive offerings to Delphi — among all the silver offerings there, his are more numerous than any other man's, and besides the silver he dedicated a vast quantity of gold, and in particular one offering worth mentioning above the rest: six golden mixing-bowls, dedicated there as his gift. Their weight is thirty talents, and they stand in the treasury of the Corinthians — though in truth this treasury does not belong to the Corinthian state, but to Cypselus, the son of Eëtion. This Gyges was the first of the barbarians known to us to dedicate votive offerings at Delphi, except for Midas, son of Gordias, king of Phrygia, who dedicated the royal throne on which he sat in judgment — a throne well worth seeing, and it stands in the same place as the bowls of Gyges. The gold and silver Gyges dedicated is called Gygian by the Delphians, after the name of the giver.

Now Gyges, as soon as he became king, led an army against Miletus and Smyrna, and took the lower town of Colophon. But no other great deed did he accomplish in his reign, which lasted thirty-eight years, so we will say no more of him than has already been said,
